_comment: Storyboard for the Bones and Muscles unit lecture video (Grade 4 Science, Cambridge 0097 Stage 4). One BEAT is one narration clip and one drawing state: the animation is timed from the measured length of each clip, so a bone lights up exactly as it is named rather than on a guessed schedule. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-science-unit-lecture.py. The skeleton and the arm are not redrawn here - they are lifted at render time out of lesson-kit/lib/science.js, so the child watches the same drawing they tap in the lesson.
title: Bones and Muscles
subtitle: Grade 4 Science
objectives: Identify some of the important bones in the human body (limited to skull, jaw, rib cage, hip, spine, leg bones and arm bones).
Know that bones move because pairs of muscles that are attached to them contract and relax.
Describe some of the important functions of skeletons (limited to protecting and supporting organs, enabling movement and giving shape to the body).
Describe the importance of movement in maintaining human health.
Make a prediction describing some possible outcomes of an enquiry.
Identify whether results support, or do not support, a prediction.
Make a conclusion from results and relate it to the scientific question being investigated.
Identify people who use science, including professionally, in their area and describe how they use science.

beats.say: Stand up. Now sit down again.
You just moved about two hundred bones, and you did not think about a single one of them.
Inside you is a frame of about two hundred bones. That frame is your skeleton. Seven of its bones are the ones to know.
The skull. A hard case of bone around your brain.
The jaw. The only bone in your head that moves. It lets you chew and talk.
The rib cage. Curved bones that guard your heart and lungs, and lift when you breathe.
The spine, or backbone. Not one long bone, but a chain of small ones. That is exactly why you can bend.
The hip bones. They join your legs to your spine, and they carry your weight.
The arm bones. One above the elbow, two below it.
And the leg bones. The thigh bone is the biggest bone in your whole body.
So what is a skeleton actually for? Four jobs.
It protects. The skull is a case round your brain. The ribs are a cage round your heart and lungs.
It supports you. Your spine, hips and legs hold you up against gravity.
It gives you your shape. You are shaped like a person, and not like a jellyfish.
And it lets you move, because muscles pull on bones.
One more thing. Bones are not dead like stones. They are alive. They grow with you, and a broken one mends itself.
But a bone cannot move itself. Muscles do that.
A muscle is joined to a bone by a tendon. When a muscle contracts, it gets shorter and fatter, and it pulls.
Watch the biceps, on the front of the upper arm. It contracts. Shorter. Fatter. And the arm bends.
beats.chip: the biceps pulls the arm up

beats.say: Now here is the part that matters most. A muscle can only pull. It can never push.
beats.banner: A muscle can only PULL. Never push.

beats.say: So how does the arm ever get straight again? It needs a second muscle, pulling the other way. The triceps, on the back of the upper arm.
Predict it first. When the triceps contracts, the arm will straighten.
Now watch. It did straighten. So the result supported our prediction.
And so, our conclusion. A muscle can only pull, so every bone that moves has a pair. One contracts while the other relaxes. Then they swap.
Muscles answer to use. Move every day and your muscles grow stronger, your bones grow harder, and your heart gets better at its job.
Sit still for weeks and all of that slips back. Walking, playing, climbing the stairs. It all counts, and it is why moving every day keeps you healthy.
People near you use this science every day.
A physiotherapist makes a weak muscle strong again, so a joint moves both ways.
A radiographer takes an X-ray of your bones, so a doctor can see a break without opening you up.
A P E teacher knows which muscles each exercise works, and why you warm up before you run.
And a paramedic keeps a broken bone still while they move you.
Seven bones. Four jobs. Muscles pull, and never push. And that is why they work in pairs.
Now go and do it yourself.
